# Preface {.unnumbered}

This companion follows the slides of **Chapter 4: Stimulated Emission Devices, Optical Amplifiers and Lasers** (Basics of
Optoelectronics, University of Trento) section by section. The slides tell the story; this book lets you **compute it**. Every
figure is made by a few lines of Python that you can unfold ("Show the Python"), copy and modify. The **live panels** (marked
with a blue bar on the left) recompute directly in your browser. They need no installation.

[![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/{{< var github_user >}}/{{< var repo >}}/blob/main/{{< var subdir >}}/notebooks/interactive_explorers.ipynb) &nbsp;Interactive explorers in Google Colab (no installation, Google account needed).

## Where this chapter sits in the course

Chapter 1 described light as a wave, Chapter 2 guided it in fibers and Chapter 3 built a source, the LED, from a forward-biased
pn junction. An LED emits by **spontaneous** emission: every photon has a random phase and direction, and the spectrum is a few
$k_BT$ wide. Chapter 4 adds the third process between light and matter, **stimulated emission**. It is the basis of optical
**amplifiers** (the erbium-doped fiber amplifier that made long-haul WDM possible, the semiconductor optical amplifier) and of
**lasers**: a gain medium inside an optical resonator. The same three ingredients, a population inversion, an optical gain
$g$ and a cavity with losses $\alpha_t$, explain the ruby, He–Ne and Nd:YAG lasers as well as the laser diodes that drive every
fiber link (Ch. 2) and are detected by the photodiodes of Ch. 5.

::: {.callout-note}
## Units in the code
The slides quote concentrations in cm$^{-3}$ and cross sections in cm$^2$, as most laser texts do. The code works in
**SI units** (m$^{-3}$, m$^2$, m$^{-1}$ for gain and loss coefficients). Photon and band energies are in **eV**. Two constants
convert: `lz.CM3 = 1e6` (cm$^{-3}$ → m$^{-3}$) and `lz.CM2 = 1e-4` (cm$^2$ → m$^2$). A gain of 1 cm$^{-1}$ is 100 m$^{-1}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Slide numbers

pages and a different numbering.
:::

## Using the code

All functions live in a small, readable module, [`laserlib.py`](laserlib.py), which you can import from your own notebooks:

```python
import laserlib as lz
lz.threshold_gain(alpha_s=0.05, L=0.4, R1=0.95, R2=1.0)     # He-Ne threshold gain, m^-1
lz.edfa_gain_uniform(0.9, 3.2e-25, 2.4e-25, 1e25, 3.0)     # g (m^-1) and G of a 3 m EDFA at 90 % inversion
```

See the appendix [Running the notebooks](running.qmd) for installation.
